newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ warns wider band to lead to higher inflation.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ warns wider band to lead to higher inflation.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has warned politicians a wider inflation target band than the current 0-2 percent would lead to higher average inflation, although it accepts that the target and the Reserve Bank Act are not set in stone.

In a 61-page briefing on the RBNZ and its role provided to all political parties, the bank said the target band should be wide enough that "the public at large could be fairly confident of the bank's ability to deliver inflation outcomes within the range most of the time".
While a narrower band would probably lack credibility a wider one would weaken the discipline on the bank.

"Moreover with a wider target range the normal pressures on policy would likely lead to inflation outcomes more commonly near the top of the range than near the bottom of the range, and average inflation correspondingly higher."
"Public trust in the commitment to price stability...is recent and fragile. It would be easy but costly to undermine that trust," the bank said in the briefing. A copy was obtained by Reuters.

The opposition Labour Party wants to widen the target to minus one to three percent while the nationalist New Zealand First Party, which holds the balance of power after the October 12 election, wants a target below the average of New Zealand's main trading partners and sustainable economic growth added to the bank's target of price stability.
The bank said the key elements of the monetary policy framework were an unambiguous goal for policy, an autonomous bank, and accountability and transparency in the conduct of monetary policy.
"The framework, however is not immutable and should be allowed to evolve through time as we learn from experience," the bank said.
It defended central bank independence as a key element even if there were changes to other components of the mix.

"It can be noted that providing the central bank with a substantial degree of operational autonomy in the formulation and implementation of monetary policy is generally a sensible arrangement even if the ultimate goal is not price stability."
It said the bank should not solely be judged on whether it achieves the 0-2 percent target.

"Although the (policy targets agreement) establishes a quantitative inflation target... it is not sensible to assess the bank's diligence or effectiveness in pursuit of the target simply on the basis of inflation outcomes.
"...Fortuitous developments may either mask lack of diligence or unfairly give the impression of inattention to the inflation target.
"Basing the assessment of policy solely on inflation outcomes opens the door for extended periods of deflection of policy from the target before remedial steps may be taken."

Turning to the inflation measure, it ruled out any other measure than one based on the CPI. It said if underlying inflation were used as the formal policy target it would need to be unambiguous and verifiable.

Even though monetary policy seemed to be too loose for the non-tradeables sector and too tight for the tradeables sector there was little the bank could do to influence the mix of interest and exchange rates as the economy adjusted to the current point in the cycle.

"Even though the bank is well aware of the very different pressures facing different sections of the economy in these circumstances, it is also aware that it cannot fundamentally change the problem. What it can do is determine whether the adjustment process will be more or less inflationary."
